answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Microsoft.DocumentDB/resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (use the Cosmos DB account resource with Kind set to MongoDB for a Mongo-compatible DocumentDB cluster).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the core CLI group 'az cosmosdb'. e.g. az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group rg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2. (az cosmosdb is part of the core az CLI, not a separate extension.)

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: resource of type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts' with properties.apiProperties.kind or kind: 'MongoDB'. Example: resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: accountName; kind: 'MongoDB'; properties: { consistencyPolicy: {...} } }. Terraform (azurerm): use azurerm_cosmosdb_account (set offer_type/api_kind to MongoDB) and azureRM provider resources like azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database for DBs/collections.

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Use a MongoDB connection string. Example (Cosmos Mongo API style): mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@. For SRV style you may see mongodb+srv://<username>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/<db>?authSource=admin&tls=true. Port for TLS is 10255 (Cosmos Mongo API); options must include SSL/TLS (ssl=true or tls=true), authSource=admin (or as provided), and replicaSet=globaldb for Cosmos Mongo API.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is billed as Cosmos-style Request Units (RUs) for provisioned throughput (manual or autoscale). There is also a serverless option for small workloads on supported APIs. Traditional vCore-based tiers (as used by managed MongoDB/vCore offerings) do not apply when you use the Mongo-compatible Cosmos DB account model.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: The Mongo-compatible endpoint uses standard Mongo auth (SCRAM username/password / database credentials). X.509 certificate auth may be supported in some managed offerings, but Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication is NOT supported for the Mongo DB wire endpoint in typical Cosmos DB Mongo API deployments — you authenticate with the Mongo user and password (SCRAM). There is no driver-side AAD token flow for Mongo endpoints; use the provided Mongo credentials or certificate methods where supported.

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for your language (e.g., pymongo for Python, the official Node.js MongoDB driver). There is no separate service-specific Mongo client; do NOT use azure-cosmos SDK for Mongo wire traffic. Use pymongo.MongoClient pointed at the provided connection string.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Index implementations available on the managed service include HNSW, IVF and DiskANN (service supports HNSW/IVF/DiskANN-backed vector indexes). Example Mongo-style createIndex I would use: db.transcripts.createIndex( { embedding: 'knnVector' }, { knnVector: { algorithm: 'hnsw', spaceType: 'cosine', dims: 1536, efConstruction: 200 } } ).

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text: either use the Mongo text index for simple text search or integrate the cluster with Azure Cognitive Search for richer full-text and cognitive indexing. Hybrid vector+text search is typically implemented by using the vector index for nearest-neighbor retrieval and combining it with text scoring (either via application-side re-ranking or an Azure Cognitive Search pipeline). There isn't a single proprietary hybrid search API — you combine vector knn retrieval and text filters/scores.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Targeted Mongo wire protocol support is MongoDB 6.x/7.0 era (many managed Mongo-compatible offerings advertise MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol). However, not all server-side MongoDB features are available: server-side JavaScript, certain admin commands, some aggregation or change-stream behaviors, and operations that rely on underlying Mongo storage-engine internals may be unsupported or behave differently. Expect differences in transactions, server-side plugins, and some admin/replica-set commands.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is no full-featured local emulator for the Mongo-compatible vector-enabled managed service. For local development use the official MongoDB Docker image (mongo:7.0) listening on 27017 for basic protocol compatibility, but vector/indexing features from the managed service will not be available locally. If you must test management or index features, run them against the live cluster.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams support depends on the managed Mongo API: historically Cosmos DB exposed a different change feed rather than Mongo change streams. For many Cosmos Mongo API deployments: Mongo change streams are not supported; instead use the Cosmos DB change feed or service-specific change mechanisms. If the service offers change streams, you may need to enable the feature or use a supported server version. (Treat change streams as likely unavailable unless explicitly documented for your cluster.)

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server to get data-plane tooling appropriate for the DocumentDB/Mongo-compatible cluster. The general azure MCP server covers Azure resource provisioning but the documentdb MCP server provides collection/index inspection and query-plan tools specifically for this service.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Historically Microsoft used the name 'Azure DocumentDB' as the original document database service; that platform evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. The Azure DocumentDB name is legacy; Azure Cosmos DB is the umbrella service. The open-source 'DocumentDB' projects are distinct and unrelated — Microsoft’s DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is a managed Microsoft service with its own engine and compatibility layers.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: The Mongo-compatible endpoint sits on the provider's managed DocumentDB/Cosmos DB engine (a Mongo wire compatibility layer over the service engine). In practice you use MongoDB drivers and most app code will be unchanged, but expect differences in billing (RUs), some unsupported server-side features, and subtle differences in query semantics and performance characteristics.

answers.question: Which database name should this sample use?
answers.answer: Use the database named 'sample_fintech_04' for everything the sample creates and reads.

answers.question: What collection and index will the sample create for transcripts and vectors?
answers.answer: Create a collection named 'transcripts'. Create a vector index on the 'embedding' field. Example command I would run: db.transcripts.createIndex( { embedding: 'knnVector' }, { knnVector: { algorithm: 'hnsw', spaceType: 'cosine', dims: 1536, efConstruction: 200 } } ).

answers.question: How will the sample connect from Python to the cluster at runtime?
answers.answer: Read the connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI and call pymongo.MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI'], tls=True, serverSelectionTimeoutMS=5000). Use admin/authSource and options exactly as provided in the environment URI; do not hardcode credentials.

answers.question: How should the sample store embeddings and metadata for each transcript chunk?
answers.answer: Store each chunk as a document with fields: { _id, source: '<pdf-filename>', timestamp: '<hh:mm:ss or page:pos>', text: '<chunk text>', embedding: [float32,...], chunk_id: '<file>-<n>' }. Use bulk inserts in batches (e.g., 500 docs) to load data efficiently.

answers.question: What query/aggregation will the sample use to retrieve nearest neighbour chunks for a query embedding?
answers.answer: Use the service's vector search aggregation stage. Example aggregation I would attempt: db.transcripts.aggregate([ { $search: { knnBeta: { vector: <queryVec>, path: 'embedding', k: 10 } } }, { $project: { score: { $meta: 'searchScore' }, text: 1, source: 1, timestamp: 1 } } ]). Then re-rank or trim results to fit the LLM context window and attach citations (source + timestamp) for each chunk.
